lesson.title: Turning a Picture Into a Number
lesson.summary: Formalizes the slope of the tangent line as the limit of the difference quotient, replacing the visual rotation of secant lines with an algebraic procedure that works for any function.
lesson.body:
The previous section built a tangent line by watching secant lines rotate into place, but "watching" is not a mathematical operation you can run on any function. This section turns that observation into a precise formula: the slope of the tangent line at a point x = a, written as a limit, is m equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(a + h) minus f(a)] divided by h, provided that limit exists. This single expression is doing exactly what the picture did, sliding a second point toward a on the curve, except now it is algebra, so it works for any function you can write down, not just ones you can graph by eye.

It helps to be precise about why the limit is necessary rather than just plugging in h = 0 directly. If you set h = 0 in the ratio [f(a + h) minus f(a)] divided by h, you get 0 divided by 0, which is undefined. The ratio is only meaningful for h close to but not equal to 0, which is exactly the situation a limit is built to handle: it describes the trend of a quantity as h approaches 0 without ever requiring h to actually reach it.

Return to f(x) = x squared at a = 3, now doing the algebra formally instead of building a numeric table. The slope of the tangent is the limit as h approaches 0 of [(3 + h) squared minus 3 squared] divided by h. Expand the numerator: (3 + h) squared equals 9 plus 6h plus h squared, and subtracting 9 leaves 6h plus h squared, which factors as h times (6 + h). Dividing by h, which is legitimate for every h in the limit except h = 0 itself, gives 6 + h. Now the expression 6 + h has no division problem left, so the limit as h approaches 0 can be found by direct substitution: 6 + 0 = 6. The slope of the tangent to y = x squared at x = 3 is exactly 6, matching the numeric evidence from the tangent line section but now proven algebraically rather than estimated from a table.

Notice that the algebra did real work here: it removed the h in the denominator before taking the limit, which is the standard move for these problems, since the raw expression is always an indeterminate 0 over 0 form at h = 0. Whenever this cancellation is possible, the limit exists and gives a genuine number for the slope.

It is also worth noting what this formula does not depend on: nothing here was specific to the number 3. The same limit, m equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(a + h) minus f(a)] divided by h, applies at any point a where the limit exists, producing whatever tangent slope belongs to that particular location on the curve. Mathematicians sometimes write this specific slope as m sub tan to distinguish it from the slope of an arbitrary line, but the subscript is just a label, the underlying number is produced by exactly the limiting process shown above, repeated at whichever a is under discussion.

The slope of the tangent at a point is more than a geometric curiosity. It is the same number that describes how fast f is changing right at x = a, which is why the next section connects this geometric slope to the idea of an instantaneous rate of change, the two threads that braid together into the formal definition of the derivative.
